questions.q: Why can't a child record's load file simply contain the parent's new Salesforce Id when the file is being prepared?
options: Salesforce assigns Ids automatically at insert time, so the new Id doesn't exist yet when the source file is being prepared
Salesforce Ids are not allowed to appear in CSV files
Child records are never allowed to reference a parent's Id under any circumstances
Salesforce Ids are always identical to the legacy system's own identifiers
questions.explain: A Salesforce record's Id is assigned automatically when it's inserted — at the point the source file is being prepared, that new Id simply doesn't exist yet, which is exactly the problem External ID fields solve.

questions.q: What does "upsert" do when a record's External ID value matches an existing record?
options: It always inserts a new record regardless of the match
It deletes the existing record and leaves nothing in its place
It updates the existing matching record instead of inserting a new one
It triggers a Hard Delete on the matching record
questions.explain: Upsert checks for a match on the External ID (or Id if no External ID exists) — if a match is found, it updates that existing record; if not, it inserts a new one.

questions.q: Why does marking an External ID field "Unique" matter for migration safety?
options: It has no real effect on migration safety
It is required before the field can be used in any formula
It automatically triggers Hard Delete behavior on duplicate values
It prevents two different source records from accidentally colliding on the same External ID value and silently overwriting each other
questions.explain: Marking the field both External ID and Unique is standard practice specifically to stop two different source records from colliding on the same value and silently overwriting one another during upsert.

questions.q: How does mapping a lookup column to a parent's External ID field (instead of its Salesforce Id) help with relationship loading?
options: It removes the need to load the parent object before the child object
It lets the child's load file reference the parent using an identifier that was known from the very beginning, without needing the parent's not-yet-assigned new Id
It automatically reorders the load sequence without any design work
It only works for self-referencing relationships, not parent-child ones
questions.explain: The parent still has to load first (sequencing doesn't go away), but the child's file never needs to know the parent's new Salesforce Id — it only needs the parent's legacy identifier, known from the start.

questions.q: A team upserts Contacts against the Salesforce Id field instead of a true legacy External ID. What symptom does this lesson say to expect?
options: The first run appears to work, but every subsequent re-run of the same file creates a new batch of duplicate records instead of matching existing ones
The very first load run fails immediately with a permissions error
No Contacts will ever be created, on any run
The records will load correctly every time, with no issues at all
questions.explain: Because the source file never contained a true Salesforce Id to match against on the first run, every re-run fails to find a match and inserts a fresh set of duplicates — the classic symptom of upserting against Id instead of a real External ID.
